title: Use-of-force expert testifies for defence at OPP officer's manslaughter trial
subtitle: A use-of-force expert testified at the trial of a Chatham-Kent OPP officer who shot a man while responding to theft of $40 of gas
article: The defence called a use-of-force expert to testify Tuesday before resting its case in the trial of a Chatham-Kent OPP officer who shot a man while responding to a theft of gas call in July 2021.
Const. Sean O'Rourke has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter in the death of Nicholas Edward -, 24, of Brantford after he was shot by the officer in the early morning of July 7, 2021.

O'Rourke and Chatham-Kent OPP Sgt. Bradley Cook responded to a report of a $40 gas theft from the Dutton ONroute. The officers were told the driver of a suspect vehicle was heading west on Highway 401 .

Court previously heard the shooting occurred after a 2003 Pontiac Sunfire, driven by Grieves, rammed into an unmarked Dodge Durango driven by O'Rourke, spun off the road and became mired in mud at the bottom of the centre median near Highgate.

While on the stand last week, O'Rourke testified to seeing a "crazed look" in Grieves' eyes as he approached the Sunfire. The officer also said he was concerned about a weapon being involved when Grieves kept looking at the car's centre console.

While his police issued Glock handgun was drawn, O'Rourke testified he tripped on the slope of the median and the momentum caused his arms, gun, head and part of his shoulder to fall through the open passenger side window of the car.
While in a panic trying to get out the car, O'Rourke testified his gun went off and the bullet hit Grieves in the right shoulder, severing two main arteries. He died later in hospital.
The officer has testified he didn't have his finger on the trigger of the weapon and doesn't know how the gun fired.
During the sixth day of the trial Tuesday, use-of-force expert Christopher Butler provided some possibilities where a Glock service revolver can unintentionally discharge.
The first are instances of mechanical malfunction where a weapon fires when there was no finger on the trigger, he said.

Butler testified this happened to him once during a training session, where it turned out a mechanical malfunction caused his weapon to fire when his finger was not in the trigger. He noted this can happen with "high mileage" weapons that have had "a lot of rounds put through them."
Butler said an "intrusion into the trigger guard" by something unintended could cause the weapon to discharge.
Third, he said it could be a case where a person believes their finger is outside the trigger guard and when something unexpected happens the finger moves to the trigger.
Butler said if someone loses their balance, they can experience a "clutch mechanism" and if their finger is on the trigger the gun will discharge.
Crown attorney Jason Nicol said to Butler during his cross-examination the realistic cause of the Glock weapon firing was "somebody pulled the trigger."
"I don't agree," Butler said.
He added it's possible there could have been a "latent mechanical malfunction" with the firearm.
However, since Butler didn't inspect the firearm, he conceded it was speculation on his part.
Court heard Butler listened to O'Rourke's testimony.
Defence lawyer Sandy Khehra asked Butler about O'Rourke being questioned why he didn't move to the right or left when he fell toward the vehicle while holding his weapon.

Citing his experience doing "real world" training with officers, Butler said it can be very difficult when something happens quickly, while in a perceived threat situation, for an officer to be able to think critically or analytically.
Butler also testified in the totality of the circumstances, it was appropriate for O'Rourke to have his weapon drawn in a ready position pointing at the car.
The trial resumes Friday when the Crown and defence make their closing submissions.
